newsitem.title: UK: Lloyds TSB seen on Australia watch.
newsitem.headline: Lloyds TSB seen on Australia watch.

text.p: Lloyds TSB is emerging as the frontrunner to follow Bank of Scotland's lead and bid for a piece of the action in Australian banking where restraints on overseas entrants are seen easing soon, analysts said.
The move comes as Sir Bruce Patullo, BoS governor and chief executive, warned other big UK finance houses they should not expect an open season on bids down under.
Up to now, the Australian Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB) has, by and large, ruled against overseas moves on home grown financial institutions.
The one major exception affecting Britain was the BoS itself which owns 51 percent of BankWest, having bought the bank in 1995 and later floated 49 pct of its shares in the Australian market.
BankWest is in the top four Australian banks along with ANZ, Westpac and National Australia, which also happens to own Scotland's Clydesdale Bank.
The Australian government is due to receive recommendations soon on relaxing the barriers to foreign ownership in Australia.
A flurry of activity is then expected and banking has been highlighted by analysts as a sector liable to attract the attention of UK financial investors in 1997.

Hugh Pye, banking analyst at BZW, said, "Australia is very similar to the UK in terms of the banks and other financial institutions. They cannot effectively be taken over except by agreement of the incumbent management."
"In saying that, one or two of the bigger banks over there could consider a bid. Things do need to happen to reduce over capacity."
He said BoS had made a wise move when it bought BankWest, a point which will not have been lost on Lloyds.

"Bank of Scotland is a long-term player and keeps very strategic horizons compared with most English banks," Pye added. "The one exception is Lloyds. It has indicated it might expand further and this could extend into an interest in what is on offer in Australia."
A Lloyds spokesperson said the bank never ruled out any prospect of a transaction if the price was right.
Pattullo told Reuters he expected the major banks in Australia to come under UK scrutiny.

"However, I cannot see the FIRB changing its policy of thoroughness when it, in turn, scrutinises any bid," he added. "We found the board to be extremely well organised and there will be no overnight mergers. It took us almost a decade to get where we are in Australia.
Sir Bruce says any UK institution looking to make a move into Australia should take note. "There will be no free for all."
